text: What does not destroy me strengthens me.
author: Friedrich Nietzsche
source: Twilight of the Idols, "Maxims and Arrows" §8 (tr. Kaufmann)

text: You shall become the person you are.
author: Friedrich Nietzsche
source: The Gay Science §270 (tr. Kaufmann)

text: Men seek retreats for themselves, houses in the country, sea-shores, and mountains; and thou too art wont to desire such things very much. But this is altogether a mark of the most common sort of men, for it is in thy power whenever thou shalt choose to retire into thyself.
author: Marcus Aurelius
source: Meditations 4.3 (Long translation)

text: In the morning when thou risest unwillingly, let this thought occur: I am rising to the work of a human being.
author: Marcus Aurelius
source: Meditations 5.1 (Long translation)

text: Do not act as if thou wert going to live ten thousand years. Death hangs over thee. While thou livest, while it is in thy power, be good.
author: Marcus Aurelius
source: Meditations 4.17 (Long translation)

text: Nothing, Lucilius, is ours, except time.
author: Seneca
source: Letters to Lucilius 1.3 (Gummere translation)

text: Men are disturbed not by things, but by the principles and notions which they form concerning things.
author: Epictetus
source: Enchiridion 5

text: If you want to improve, be content to be thought foolish and stupid with regard to external things.
author: Epictetus
source: Enchiridion 13

text: Remember that you are an actor in a drama, of such a kind as the author pleases to make it.
author: Epictetus
source: Enchiridion 17

text: Purity of heart is to will one thing.
author: Søren Kierkegaard
source: Purity of Heart Is to Will One Thing (1847), title discourse, tr. Douglas V. Steere (1938)

text: Boredom is the root of all evil.
author: Søren Kierkegaard
source: Either/Or, Part One, "The Rotation of Crops" (1843), tr. Howard V. Hong and Edna H. Hong

text: The struggle itself toward the heights is enough to fill a man's heart. One must imagine Sisyphus happy.
author: Albert Camus
source: The Myth of Sisyphus, concluding section (trans. Justin O'Brien, 1955)

text: The absurd is born of this confrontation between the human need and the unreasonable silence of the world.
author: Albert Camus
source: The Myth of Sisyphus, Part One, 'An Absurd Reasoning' (trans. Justin O'Brien, 1955)

text: I opened myself to the gentle indifference of the world.
author: Albert Camus
source: The Stranger, Part Two, chapter 5 (trans. Matthew Ward)

text: There are more things to admire in men than to despise.
author: Albert Camus
source: The Plague, Part Five (trans. Stuart Gilbert)

text: Everything can be taken from a man but one thing: the last of the human freedoms—to choose one's attitude in any given set of circumstances, to choose one's own way.
author: Viktor Frankl
source: Man's Search for Meaning, Part One (Experiences in a Concentration Camp)

text: Who looks outside dreams; who looks inside awakes.
author: Carl Jung
source: Letter to Fanny Bowditch, 22 October 1916, The Letters of C. G. Jung, Vol. 1 (1906-1950), p. 33

text: Blind are the eyes of anyone who does not know his own heart, and I always recommend the application of a little psychology so that he can understand things like the gospel still better.
author: Carl Jung
source: Letter to Julia Schmid-Lohner, 20 May 1947, The Letters of C. G. Jung, Vol. 1 (1906-1950)

text: The suffering is an indispensable part of it. Every real solution is only reached by intense suffering.
author: Carl Jung
source: Letter to P. W. Martin, 20 August 1937, The Letters of C. G. Jung, Vol. 1 (1906-1950), pp. 233-234

text: If a man knows the wherefore of his existence, then the manner of it can take care of itself.
author: Friedrich Nietzsche
source: Twilight of the Idols (trans. Anthony M. Ludovici), "Maxims and Arrows" section 12

text: The eternal sand-glass of existence will ever be turned once more, and thou with it, thou speck of dust!
author: Friedrich Nietzsche
source: The Gay Science (The Joyful Wisdom; trans. Thomas Common), aphorism 341, "The Heaviest Burden"

text: Creating—that is the great salvation from suffering, and life’s alleviation.
author: Friedrich Nietzsche
source: Thus Spoke Zarathustra (trans. Thomas Common), Second Part, chapter XXIV "In the Happy Isles"

text: Not backward can the Will will; that it cannot break time and time’s desire—that is the Will’s lonesomest tribulation.
author: Friedrich Nietzsche
source: Thus Spoke Zarathustra (trans. Thomas Common), Second Part, chapter XLII "Redemption"

text: I swear, gentlemen, that to be too conscious is an illness—a real thorough-going illness.
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
source: Notes from Underground, Part I, Chapter II (trans. Constance Garnett)

text: Why, suffering is the sole origin of consciousness.
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
source: Notes from Underground, Part I, Chapter IX (trans. Constance Garnett)

text: Almost every criminal is subject to a failure of will and reasoning power by a childish and phenomenal heedlessness, at the very instant when prudence and caution are most essential.
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
source: Crime and Punishment, Part I, Chapter VI (trans. Constance Garnett)

text: Pain and suffering are always inevitable for a large intelligence and a deep heart.
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
source: Crime and Punishment, Part III, Chapter V (trans. Constance Garnett)

text: Above all, don’t lie to yourself. The man who lies to himself and listens to his own lie comes to such a pass that he cannot distinguish the truth within him, or around him, and so loses all respect for himself and for others.
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
source: The Brothers Karamazov, Book II, Chapter II (trans. Constance Garnett)

text: Fathers and teachers, I ponder, “What is hell?” I maintain that it is the suffering of being unable to love.
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
source: The Brothers Karamazov, Book VI, Chapter III (trans. Constance Garnett)

text: Unless suffering is the direct and immediate object of life, our existence must entirely fail of its aim.
author: Arthur Schopenhauer
source: Studies in Pessimism (T. Bailey Saunders tr.), essay "On the Sufferings of the World", opening paragraph

text: No little part of the torment of existence lies in this, that Time is continually pressing upon us, never letting us take breath, but always coming after us, like a taskmaster with a whip.
author: Arthur Schopenhauer
source: Studies in Pessimism (T. Bailey Saunders tr.), essay "On the Sufferings of the World"

text: So a great intellect sinks to the level of an ordinary one, as soon as it is interrupted and disturbed, its attention distracted and drawn off from the matter in hand; for its superiority depends upon its power of concentration--of bringing all its strength to bear upon one theme, in the same way as a concave mirror collects into one point all the rays of light that strike upon it.
author: Arthur Schopenhauer
source: Studies in Pessimism (T. Bailey Saunders tr.), essay "On Noise"

text: The delight which a man has in hoping for and looking forward to some special satisfaction is a part of the real pleasure attaching to it enjoyed in advance. This is afterwards deducted; for the more we look forward to anything, the less satisfaction we find in it when it comes.
author: Arthur Schopenhauer
source: Studies in Pessimism (T. Bailey Saunders tr.), essay "On the Sufferings of the World"

text: It is played that a man may come to understand himself, that he may see what it is that he seeks and has sought to be; what he wants, and what, therefore, he is.
author: Arthur Schopenhauer
source: On Human Nature (T. Bailey Saunders tr.), section "Character"

text: And I may say, further, that a certain amount of care or pain or trouble is necessary for every man at all times. A ship without ballast is unstable and will not go straight.
author: Arthur Schopenhauer
source: Studies in Pessimism (T. Bailey Saunders tr.), essay "On the Sufferings of the World"

text: Lay hold of today’s task, and you will not need to depend so much upon tomorrow’s.
author: Seneca
source: Letters to Lucilius, Letter I (trans. Richard M. Gummere)

text: The primary indication, to my thinking, of a well-ordered mind is a man’s ability to remain in one place and linger in his own company.
author: Seneca
source: Letters to Lucilius, Letter II (trans. Richard M. Gummere)

text: And in reading of many books is distraction.
author: Seneca
source: Letters to Lucilius, Letter II (trans. Richard M. Gummere)

text: I should prefer to be free from torture; but if the time comes when it must be endured, I shall desire that I may conduct myself therein with bravery, honour, and courage.
author: Seneca
source: Letters to Lucilius, Letter LXVII, "On Ill-Health and Endurance of Suffering" (trans. Richard M. Gummere)

text: Life is long enough, if you know how to use it.
author: Seneca
source: On the Shortness of Life, section II (trans. Aubrey Stewart, in Project Gutenberg eBook #64576, Minor Dialogues)
